issues.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to explain injuries on an accused person does not require rejection of all prosecution evidence when evidence of separate attacks is independently corroborated.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses did not explain the minor injuries sustained by one accused person.
The courts below rejected the prosecution account of the initial attack, but accepted evidence of later attacks on two deceased persons at separate locations.
Blood found at the location of one attack corroborated the evidence about that attack, and an independent witness testified about the other attack.
The Supreme Court found no valid basis to reject that corroborated evidence.
issues.conclusion: The unexplained injuries did not require the Court to discard the prosecution evidence as a whole; the corroborated evidence about the separate attacks could be accepted.
issues.legal_principle: An accused person’s unexplained injuries may require careful scrutiny of prosecution evidence, but do not automatically make the entire prosecution case untruthful or establish self-defence. The Court applied Mohar Rai v. State of Bihar and Ugar Ahir v. State of Bihar, including the principle that falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus is neither a sound rule of law nor a rule of practice.

predicates.criminal_case: The prosecution tried people for criminal offences arising from an alleged violent incident.
predicates.accused_injuries_unexplained: The prosecution witnesses did not explain injuries sustained by an accused person.
predicates.separate_attack_corroborated_by_physical: Physical evidence at the scene corroborated testimony about an attack separate from the initial encounter.
predicates.separate_attack_supported_by_independent: A witness with no shown connection of friendship or enmity to either side testified about an attack separate from the initial encounter.

issues.definition: When a criminal case includes unexplained injuries to an accused person but a separate attack is corroborated by physical evidence or an independent witness, the corroborated evidence may still be accepted.

issues.legal_issue: Omissions in a brief police report or a dying declaration do not necessarily undermine an account of an incident when the documents were made in circumstances that explain their lack of detail and other evidence supports the account.
material_facts: The police report was a brief intimation prepared by a head constable who was not an eyewitness and who gathered information from people at the injured persons’ home.
The report did not describe attacks at three separate locations.
The injured person’s dying declaration was cryptic, and he was in a precarious condition when he made it.
The prosecution account of attacks at separate locations was supported by blood evidence and witness testimony.
issues.conclusion: The omissions in the report and dying declaration did not justify rejecting the prosecution account of attacks at separate locations.
issues.legal_principle: The significance of an omission depends on the circumstances in which the statement was made. A brief report based on information gathered by a non-eyewitness, and a cryptic declaration made by a person in a precarious condition, need not contain a detailed account; the Court relied on the corroborating evidence in assessing the account.

predicates.criminal_case: The prosecution presented an account of a violent incident in a criminal case.
predicates.brief_report_made_by_nonwitness: A police officer who did not witness the incident prepared a brief report from information gathered from others.
predicates.declaration_made_while_injured_person_wa: An injured person made a declaration while in a precarious physical condition.
predicates.account_supported_by_other_evidence: Other evidence, including physical evidence or witness testimony, supported the account of the incident.

issues.definition: When a criminal account is supported by other evidence, omissions in a non-eyewitness’s brief report or in a declaration made by a precariously injured person do not undermine that account.

issues.legal_issue: An independent witness’s evidence is not discredited merely because the witness’s presence is challenged as improbable or the witness implicated more accused persons than the appellate court ultimately found proved.
material_facts: A witness testified that he saw the attack on one deceased person while cutting grass near a river.
He explained that he went there because good grass was available at that location.
The witness identified all the accused as participants in the attack, but the High Court acquitted some of them because their names were absent from another injured person’s dying declaration.
That injured person was hovering between life and death when he made the declaration.
The witness was not shown to be friendly with the victims’ group or hostile to the accused.
issues.conclusion: The criticisms did not provide a valid reason to reject the independent witness’s evidence about the attack.
issues.legal_principle: A witness’s presence and credibility must be assessed in light of the explanation given and the circumstances of the evidence. The Court held that the availability of good grass answered the challenge to the witness’s presence, and that the omission of names from a declaration made by a person hovering between life and death did not invalidate the witness’s testimony.

predicates.criminal_case: The testimony was offered in a criminal case concerning an alleged attack.
predicates.independent_witness_testified_to_attack: A witness not shown to favour one side or be hostile to the other testified about an attack.
predicates.witness_explained_presence_at_scene: The witness gave an explanation for being at the location where the attack occurred.
predicates.omitted_names_came_from_precarious_decla: The criticism that some accused were not named rested on a declaration made by an injured person in a precarious condition.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, an independent witness’s testimony about an attack is not rejected on the stated criticisms when the witness explained being at the scene or the omitted names came from a precarious declaration.

issues.legal_issue: The fact that the accused side first informed the police does not by itself make the prosecution account unreliable when the victims’ side had urgent reasons to attend to the injured and the police gathered information soon afterward.
material_facts: The accused side informed the police several hours after the incident but did not mention the injuries to the victims.
One victim had died at the scene, and two others were in precarious condition.
The victims’ relatives were attending to them rather than going to the police station.
A head constable arrived within a few hours and gathered information about the incident.
issues.conclusion: The accused side’s being the first to inform the police, and the victims’ side not independently reporting the incident, did not make the prosecution account unreliable.
issues.legal_principle: The failure of a victim’s side to report an incident must be assessed in context. The Court considered the serious condition of the victims, the relatives’ attention to them, the accused side’s failure to mention the victims’ injuries in its report, and the police officer’s arrival within hours.

rule.if: criminal_case and accused_side_reported_first and (victims_relatives_attended_to_critically_injured_people or police_gathered_information_soon_after)

predicates.criminal_case: The parties’ competing accounts of a violent incident were considered in a criminal case.
predicates.accused_side_reported_first: A person from the accused side informed the police before anyone from the victims’ side did.
predicates.victims_relatives_attended_to_critically: Relatives of the victims were occupied with attending to people who were dead or seriously injured.
predicates.police_gathered_information_soon_after: A police officer arrived and gathered information within a few hours of the incident.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, an accused side’s first report does not make the prosecution account unreliable when the victims’ relatives were attending to the critically injured or the police gathered information soon after.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily reassess evidence in a criminal appeal from a High Court unless the High Court overlooked material evidence or approached the case from a wholly wrong point of view.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the High Court’s confirmation of convictions after it had assessed the evidence and acquitted some accused persons.
The Supreme Court found no material evidence that the High Court had failed to consider and no wholly wrong approach to the case.
The Court found the criticisms of the High Court’s judgment invalid.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not disturb the High Court’s assessment of the evidence, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: In a criminal case, the Supreme Court does not review the evidence merely because a party challenges the High Court’s assessment; review is warranted if material evidence was not considered or the High Court approached the case from a wholly wrong point of view.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_high_court and not material_evidence_overlooked and not wholly_wrong_approach

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_high_court: A party brought a criminal appeal to the Supreme Court challenging a High Court’s assessment of evidence.
predicates.material_evidence_overlooked: The High Court failed to take material evidence into consideration.
predicates.wholly_wrong_approach: The High Court approached the case from a wholly wrong point of view.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal from a High Court, its evidence assessment is left undisturbed when no material evidence was overlooked and its approach was not wholly wrong.
